paper_metadata.title: Efficient Hamiltonian Simulation for Solving Option Price Dynamics

summary: The paper proposes a gate-based digital quantum algorithm for Black-Scholes option pricing by mapping the PDE to a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and simulating it with QFT/QSP plus ancilla-based unitary dilation. It reports simulations using 9 qubits and an expected post-selection success probability above 60%, but does not demonstrate a practical quantum advantage over classical methods.

experiments.description: Digital quantum simulation of the Black-Scholes PDE for European put option pricing using Hamiltonian simulation with QFT/QSP, including ancilla-based unitary dilation and post-selection; evaluated in simulation for increasing qubit counts and compared against the analytical solution.

algorithm.variant: Hamiltonian simulation of Black-Scholes dynamics via QFT and quantum signal processing with unitary dilation
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Initial state prepared from the European put payoff function, duplicated symmetrically to enforce periodic boundary conditions

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Spatial coordinate x discretized on Nx=2^n grid points; option payoff encoded in amplitudes over position basis states |x_j>; one extra ancilla qubit used for unitary dilation/post-selection
problem_formulation.objective_function: Solve the Black-Scholes PDE by mapping it to a non-Hermitian Schrödinger-like equation and simulating the propagator to recover option prices
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Unitary dilation with one ancilla qubit; post-selection on ancilla state |0_E>; periodic boundary conditions enforced by duplicating the initial condition

problem_instance.description: European put option pricing under the Black-Scholes model

dataset_specification.parameters: S_max=150, K=50, sigma=0.2, r=0.04, T=1 year

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Change of variables S=e^x; time reversal τ=T-t; discretization of x on a uniform grid; payoff duplicated symmetrically around x=0 to mitigate boundary effects
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Numerical convergence and discretization-error study versus analytical Black-Scholes solution for different qubit counts; success probability of post-selection analyzed as a function of parameters

hardware.framework: Qiskit (implied by gate-based quantum-circuit context is not explicitly stated; no framework named in the excerpt)

implementation_details.classical_solver: Analytical Black-Scholes solution for validation; finite-difference discretization used for comparison
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Construct payoff state; discretize position/momentum operators; apply QFT-based diagonalization
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Post-select ancilla |0_E>; measure position basis to recover option price amplitudes; compare against analytical solution

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: convergence/error decreases with increasing qubit count

speedup_claims.factor: optimal sparse Hamiltonian simulation; O(td||H||_max + log(1/ε)/log log(1/ε))
speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical discretization / sparse Hamiltonian simulation baselines
speedup_claims.conditions: fault-tolerant quantum computer; Black-Scholes Hamiltonian treated as 1-sparse after QFT diagonalization
speedup_claims.caveats: This is an algorithmic complexity claim, not an end-to-end empirical speedup over classical option-pricing methods.

speedup_claims.conditions: for amplitude estimation in the post-processing step
speedup_claims.caveats: Mentioned as a general property of amplitude estimation; not specifically benchmarked in this paper's experiment.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(td||H||_max + log(1/ϵ)/log log(1/ϵ)) for QSP sparse Hamiltonian simulation; QFT subroutine O(n log n)
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Finite-difference / matrix-exponentiation style classical discretizations discussed as O(T_steps 2^n) or O(2^n) in the comparison table

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Fault-tolerant gate-based quantum computer with enough logical qubits to run the Hamiltonian simulation and post-selection; the paper cites 9 qubits for the toy/illustrative simulation and discusses QSP asymptotics.
